title: Cloud Data Migration
seoTitle: Design a System to Migrate Petabytes of Data to the Cloud
description: Design a large-scale data migration service — parallel chunked transfers, checksums and verification, resumability, bandwidth control, and live cutover with change sync.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is Cloud Data Migration?
blocks.text: Migration services move large datasets — petabytes of files from an on-premises data centre or another cloud — into cloud object storage, verifying every byte and keeping the copy in sync until applications switch over.

items: Users should be able to create a migration job from a source (on-prem file servers, another bucket) to a destination bucket.
The system should copy all objects, preserving metadata, and verify integrity.
Jobs should show progress and per-object errors, and be resumable.
The system should support incremental syncs so changes made during migration are copied before cutover.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Throughput: saturate available bandwidth (e.g. 10-100 Gbps) using many parallel workers.
Correctness: no silent corruption or missed files; every object verified.
Fault tolerant: worker or network failures resume without recopying completed data.
Controllable: bandwidth limits so production traffic on the source isn't harmed.
**Job**: source, destination, filters, schedule, bandwidth limit, status.
**Manifest entry**: one object to copy — path, size, mtime, checksum, state.
**Task**: a batch of manifest entries (or chunks of a large file) assigned to a worker.
**Agent**: a worker running near the source with network access to both ends.

blocks.text: 1) Create a job and build a manifest

A **Coordinator** lists the source (in parallel, by directory) and writes a **manifest** of objects to copy into a database. Listing billions of files is itself a big job, so it is split across workers too.

Agents lease tasks from the coordinator, read objects from the source and upload them with **multipart uploads** (large files split into chunks uploaded in parallel). Each chunk's checksum is sent with the upload so the destination rejects corrupted parts; after completion the agent compares the whole-object checksum, then marks the manifest entry done.

The manifest is the source of truth: entries move from `PENDING → IN_PROGRESS → VERIFIED` (or `FAILED` with an error). If an agent dies, its task leases expire and are reassigned; completed parts of multipart uploads are reused rather than resent.

Later passes re-list the source and copy only objects whose size, mtime or checksum changed since the last pass. Each pass gets smaller; at cutover, writes to the source are frozen briefly, a final sync runs, and applications switch to the cloud.

approach.text: Run one `cp -r` from a single machine.

challenges.text: Limited by one machine's network and disk; one failure restarts everything.

blocks.title: Many agents, parallel chunks, small-file batching

approach.text: Scale out agents near the source. Large files go as parallel multipart chunks; millions of tiny files are batched per task (and optionally packed) to amortise per-request overhead. A token-bucket limiter per agent enforces the bandwidth cap and can follow a schedule (faster at night).

challenges.text: Per-object API overhead dominates for small files, and destination rate limits per prefix may require spreading key names.

blocks.text: 2) How do we guarantee nothing is lost or corrupted?

Verify end to end: checksum at the source, per-chunk checksums during upload, and a whole-object checksum comparison at the destination. After the copy, run a **reconciliation**: compare source and destination listings (count, sizes, checksums) and report any differences. Never mark a job complete on "no errors seen" alone.

quiz.question: What is the manifest used for?
options: Tracking every object to copy and its state, enabling progress and resume
quiz.explanation: It's the source of truth for what's done and what remains.

quiz.question: How do you reduce downtime at cutover?
options: Copy everything during a long outage
Run incremental syncs until the delta is tiny, then freeze writes for a final pass
quiz.explanation: Each pass shrinks; the final freeze is short.

quiz.question: Why batch many small files per task?
options: Per-object overhead dominates throughput for tiny files

quiz.question: What proves the migration is complete?
options: A reconciliation comparing source and destination counts, sizes and checksums
quiz.explanation: Positive verification catches silently missed objects.
